title: Helium-Neon (He-Ne) Laser
short_intro: The Helium-Neon laser is a continuous-wave gas laser that utilizes a mixture of helium and neon gases as the active medium. It typically operates at a primary emission wavelength of 632.8 nm in the visible red region, pumped by an electrical DC discharge.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Working principle of lasers, population inversion, optical pumping via electric discharge, pumping mechanism in gas lasers, and basic identification of the active medium and output wavelength.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Detailed energy level diagram of the He-Ne system, resonant energy transfer between He and Ne atoms, Doppler broadening of spectral lines, longitudinal and transverse modes (TEM_{00}), and cavity resonance conditions.

prerequisites: Energy states and Bohr's atomic model
Spontaneous and stimulated emission, Einstein A and B coefficients

concept_notes.heading: Active Medium and Gas Mixture Ratio
bullets: The active medium consists of a mixture of helium and neon gases enclosed in a quartz discharge tube.
The typical partial pressure ratio of helium to neon is maintained at approximately 10:1.
Helium acts as the primary excitation medium while neon provides the laser active energy levels.

concept_notes.heading: Pumping Mechanism and Resonant Energy Transfer
bullets: Free electrons accelerated by an electric DC discharge collide with helium atoms, exciting them to high-lying metastable states (2^1S and 2^3S).
Excited helium atoms collide non-radiatively with unexcited neon atoms, transferring energy due to nearly matching excitation energies.
This resonant collisional transfer selectively populates the 3s and 2s levels of neon, achieving population inversion relative to lower lying p-levels.

concept_notes.heading: Laser Transitions and Emission Wavelengths
bullets: The primary visible laser transition occurs from the Ne(3s_2) to Ne(2p_4) state, yielding coherent radiation at 632.8 nm.
Other infrared transitions also occur in the He-Ne system, notably at 1.15 um and 3.39 um.
Selective mirrors coated for 632.8 nm are used in the optical cavity to suppress infrared lasing and favor the visible red output.

concept_notes.heading: De-excitation and Ground State Repopulation
bullets: From the lower laser level (2p states), neon atoms rapidly decay radiatively to the 1s metastable states.
De-excitation from the 1s state to the absolute ground state (1s^0) occurs primarily through non-radiative collisions with the inner walls of the narrow discharge tube.
A narrow tube diameter is crucial to ensure fast de-excitation of lower states and prevent bottlenecking.

derivations.title: Optical Cavity Resonance Frequency Condition
derivations.conditions: Fabry-Perot resonator of length L filled with a medium of refractive index mu
steps: For a standing wave to form inside the optical cavity, an integer multiple of half-wavelengths must equal the cavity optical path length.
Condition equation: 2 \mu L = q \lambda, where q is a large integer representing the longitudinal mode number.
Expressing wavelength in terms of frequency: \lambda = \frac{c}{\nu}, where c is the speed of light in vacuum.
Substitute into the resonance condition: 2 \mu L = q \frac{c}{\nu}, yielding \nu = \frac{q c}{2 \mu L}.
The frequency separation between adjacent longitudinal modes (Delta \nu) is obtained by setting Delta q = 1.

derivations.title: Doppler Broadening of the Laser Transition
derivations.conditions: Thermal motion of emitting neon atoms at absolute temperature T
steps: Due to thermal Maxwell-Boltzmann velocity distribution, emitting atoms possess a velocity component v along the line of sight.
The emitted frequency is Doppler shifted according to \nu = \nu_0 \left(1 \pm \frac{v}{c}\right).
The root-mean-square thermal velocity is given by v_{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{k_B T}{M}}, where M is the mass of the neon atom.
The full width at half maximum (FWHM) of the Gaussian gain profile due to Doppler broadening is expressed as \Delta \nu_D.
Evaluating the Doppler width gives \Delta \nu_D = \nu_0 \sqrt{\frac{8 k_B T \ln 2}{M c^2}}.

graphs_and_experiments.title: He-Ne Energy Level Diagram
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Parallel horizontal energy level lines for He (showing 2^1S and 2^3S levels) and Ne (showing 3s, 2p, and 1s levels) with upward electron excitation arrows and downward radiative laser transition arrows.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates resonant collisional energy transfer from helium to neon atoms and highlights the 632.8 nm laser transition.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in PGT descriptive questions to explain population inversion mechanisms in gas lasers.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Doppler Broadened Gain Profile and Cavity Modes
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A broad bell-shaped Gaussian curve representing the Doppler gain profile with multiple equally spaced vertical spikes inside representing discrete longitudinal cavity modes.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows that only those longitudinal modes whose frequencies fall within the gain profile threshold can lase simultaneously.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in conceptual multiple-choice questions regarding multi-mode laser output and spectral bandwidth.

graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the physical layout of a continuous-wave gas laser system and polarization control using Brewster windows.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Evaluated in apparatus identification and working principle questions in TGT/PGT examinations.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the frequency separation between adjacent longitudinal modes of a He-Ne laser having an optical cavity length of 30 cm. Take speed of light c = 3 x 10^8 m/s.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: Cavity length L = 30 cm = 0.3 m, refractive index \mu = 1.
Recall the longitudinal mode frequency spacing formula: \Delta \nu = \frac{c}{2 L}.
Calculate the final value: \Delta \nu = \frac{3 \times 10^8}{0.6} = 5 \times 10^8 \text{ Hz} = 500 \text{ MHz}.

solved_numericals.question: A He-Ne laser operates at 632.8 nm. If the Doppler broadened gain linewidth is 1.5 GHz, estimate the coherence length of the laser output assuming single-mode operation governed by this linewidth.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: Wavelength \lambda = 632.8 nm, linewidth \Delta \nu = 1.5 \text{ GHz} = 1.5 \times 10^9 \text{ Hz}, c = 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}.
Use the coherence length approximation formula: L_c \approx \frac{c}{\Delta \nu}.

solved_numericals.question: Determine the approximate mode number q for a He-Ne laser operating at \lambda = 632.8 nm with a cavity length L = 50 cm. Assume refractive index \mu = 1.
solution_steps: Recall the resonance condition: 2 L = q \lambda.
Rearrange to solve for mode number q: q = \frac{2 L}{\lambda}.
Substitute the given values: L = 0.5 \text{ m}, \lambda = 632.8 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes a uniform refractive index (mu = 1) inside the active discharge region.
Neglects intra-cavity diffraction losses and mirror transmission losses in elementary gain threshold calculations.
Limitation: He-Ne laser output power is relatively low (typically 1 mW to 50 mW) compared to solid-state or CO_2 lasers due to low discharge efficiency.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Helium atoms directly emit the laser beam in a He-Ne laser.
common_misconceptions.correct: Neon atoms emit the laser photons.
common_misconceptions.why: Helium atoms serve only to absorb discharge energy and transfer it collisionally to neon atoms, which provide the actual laser active transitions.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The 632.8 nm line is the only transition possible in a He-Ne laser.
common_misconceptions.correct: Infrared transitions at 1.15 um and 3.39 um also exist.
common_misconceptions.why: The laser cavity mirrors are specifically coated to introduce high losses for infrared wavelengths, forcing oscillation only at the 632.8 nm visible red wavelength.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Population inversion in He-Ne requires optical pumping with a flashlamp.
common_misconceptions.correct: Population inversion is achieved via electrical discharge pumping and resonant collisional transfer.
common_misconceptions.why: Gas lasers like He-Ne utilize DC electrical discharges rather than optical lamps for excitation.

quick_revision: Active medium in He-Ne laser: Mixture of Helium and Neon in 10:1 ratio.
Pumping mechanism: Electric DC discharge combined with resonant collisional energy transfer.
Lower laser state depopulation: Requires narrow discharge tube diameter for fast wall collisions.
Longitudinal mode frequency separation: Delta \nu = c / (2 L).
